title: Observer Activity Report - International Maritime Organization (IMO) - 2025

Instructions for submitting Observer reports 
Introduction 
This document provides the reporting template and instructions for Observers to report 
during the 2023 - 2025 Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic Council. 

The deadline for submission is 1 December 2024. 
 

Role of Observers 
The role and responsibilities of Observers, as well as criteria for admission to the Arctic 
Council, can be found in the “Arctic Council Rules of Procedure” (Annex 2) and the 
“Observer Manual for Subsidiary Bodies.” 

The primary role of Observers is to observe the work of the Arctic Council. Observers 
contribute to the Arctic Council primarily through engagement at the level of Working 
Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Observers are invited to the meetings and 
other activities of the Arctic Council unless the Senior Arctic Officials decide otherwise. 
Observers may also propose projects through an Arctic State or a Permanent Participant. 

Report submission 
Observer reports should include the relevant information described below and in the 
template. 

(a) A description of the Observer’s contributions to the work of the Arctic Council since 
the time of the Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years, with 
special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies through project participation 
and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent Participants; 

(b) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s future plans to contribute to the work of 
the Arctic Council, with special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies 
through project participation and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent 
Participants; and, 

(c) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s contributions to other aspects of the 
Arctic Council and its goals not covered in the previous sections since the time of the 
Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years. 

 

Observer reports should be submitted electronically to the Arctic Council Secretariat via 
email: acs@arctic-council.org not later than 1 December 2024. Please bear in mind while 
preparing your report that all Observer reports will be published online in the Observer 
section of the Arctic Council online Library (OAR) following the Chairship transition. 

If an Observer fails to submit a report, the Arctic Council will consider this to mean that the 
Observer is no longer interested in maintaining its status as an accredited Observer to 
the Arctic Council.

Observer Report 
Please describe in no more than two pages your State’s or Organization’s contributions to 
the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups since 
the time of your most recent report, or in the previous two years. Please highlight 
contributions to specific projects, such as through proposals, concept development, in- 
kind and financial support, and hosting of meetings. Please detail any collaboration with 
Permanent Participants, such as project proposal endorsement and support. 

General 
 
IMO submitted its first observer report on 25 November 2020 which provided some detailed information about 
IMO and its history in contributing to the work of the Arctic Council, primarily by means of developing 
regulations and guidance for ships and their crews operating in polar waters, including Arctic waters. IMO's 
second observer report was submitted on 1 June 2022 outlining relevant regulatory developments and 
technical cooperation activities, as well as IMO's engagement with the Arctic Council. 
 
The most important IMO instrument addressing ship safety and protection of the marine environment with 
respect to the Arctic, and polar waters in general, is the International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters 
(Polar Code). It sets out additional requirements for ships subject to SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW when such 
ships intend to operate in polar waters. 
 
SOLAS, MARPOL and the Polar Code are complemented by several non-mandatory guidelines to facilitate 
their implementation. It should be noted that IMO continuously assesses the appropriateness and fit-for-
purpose provisions in its instruments to determine the need for amending them. Given the overlapping 
membership between Arctic Council States and IMO Member States, there is regular information exchange 
between the two organizations. Arctic Council member and observer States, which are also IMO Member 
States, provide technical input to IMO meetings, helping enhance ship safety and protect the marine 
environment through IMO instruments. 
 
Since the previous observer report, work at IMO has been completed or is ongoing under the following outputs 
which directly relate to regulatory work with respect to Arctic shipping: 
 

- Safety measures for non-SOLAS ships operating in polar waters (ongoing) 
- Reduction of the impact on the Arctic of Black Carbon emissions from international shipping 

(ongoing) 
- Development of measures to reduce risks of use and carriage of heavy fuel oil as fuel by ships 

in Arctic waters (completed) 
- Identification and protection of special areas, ECAs and PSSAs (continuous) 

 
In addition to the above, several safety and environmental provisions have been or are currently being 
developed which will strengthen the regulatory framework for ships in general, including those operating in 
polar waters. These include, for example, the Revised guidelines for the reduction of underwater noise from 
commercial shipping to address adverse impacts on marine life (MEPC.1/Circ.906/Rev.1), the Action plan for 
the reduction of underwater noise from commercial shipping (MEPC 82/17/Add.1, annex 8), and the 
dissemination of the Guidelines for Underwater Radiated Noise Reduction in Inuit Nunaat and the Arctic by 
means of a circular (MEPC.1/Circ.907). 
 
The paragraphs below summarize IMO's collaborative activities with the Arctic Council, as well as regulatory 
developments since 1 June 2022. 
 
Arctic Council/PAME and other working groups 
 
IMO's Maritime Safety Division (Director MSD) and Marine Environment Protection Division (Director MED), 
as appropriate, regularly attend meetings of the Senior Arctic Officials (SAO). In addition, IMO has been 
working closely with PAME on many occasions with various IMO staff attending and contributing to PAME 
meetings and its working groups. IMO officers have also participated remotely and presented at ACAP, and 
liaised with EPPR. In all engagements in Arctic Council projects IMO endeavours to fully involve Permanent 
Participants.

Polar maritime seminars 
 
IMO and The Nautical Institute jointly organized the Polar Maritime Seminar at IMO Headquarters (31 October 
to 1 November 2022). The Seminar provided an update on Polar shipping developments, including vessel 
activity trends, regulations and governance. 
 
IMO and Norway as Chair of the Arctic Council, in cooperation with PAME, are organizing another Polar 
Maritime Seminar due to be hosted at IMO Headquarters (23 and 24 January 2025) 
 
IMO regulatory developments 
 
IMO has recently completed or is currently developing new regulations and guidance which either directly or 
indirectly relate to improving ship safety and the protection of the marine environment in the Arctic. These 
include: 

 
With respect to safety of non-SOLAS ships: 
 
.1 adoption of amendments to SOLAS chapter XIV (by means of resolution MSC.532(107)) and 

the Polar Code (by means of resolution MSC.538(107)) introducing mandatory provisions 
concerning navigation and voyage planning for certain types of non-SOLAS ships, namely 
fishing vessels of 24 metres in length overall and above, pleasure yachts of 300 gross 
tonnage and upwards not engaged in trade, and cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage and 
upwards but below 500 gross tonnage; 

 
 With respect to life-saving appliances on board ships 
 

.2 approval of Revised interim guidelines on life-saving appliances and arrangements for ships 
operating in polar waters (MSC.1/Circ.1614/Rev.1); 

 
 With respect to training and welfare of seafarers 
 
.3 adoption of the revised annex to the 1995-F Convention (by means of resolution 

MSC.561(108)) and of the new STCW-F Code (resolution MSC.562(108)) to improve fishing 
vessel safety; 

 
.4 approval of the methodology, roadmap, and list of specific areas for the comprehensive 

review of the STCW Convention and Code, which will include consideration of proposals to 
incorporate recommendations on Polar Code training programmes; 

 
 With respect to places of refuge 

 
.5 adoption of revised Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance (resolution 

A.1184(33)); 
 
 With respect to measures to protect the marine environment 
 
.6 adoption of amendments to MARPOL Annex VI concerning the designation of the Canadian 

Arctic and the Norwegian Sea as ECAs for Nitrogen Oxides, Sulphur Oxides and Particulate 
Matter (resolution MEPC.392(82)); 

 
.7 adoption of Guidance on best practice on recommendatory goal-based control measures to 

reduce the impact on the Arctic of Black Carbon emissions from international shipping 
(resolution MEPC.393(82)); 

 
.8 adoption of Guidelines on recommendatory Black Carbon emission measurement, 

monitoring and reporting (resolution MEPC.394(82)); and 
 
.9 approval of Guidelines on mitigation measures to reduce risks of use and carriage for use of 

heavy fuel oil as fuel by ships in Arctic waters (MEPC.1/Circ.915).

Contribution to PAME Projects 
 
Fishing vessel safety 
 
IMO, together with Iceland and Spain is co-leading the project ‘Raising awareness in the Arctic Council of the 
provisions of the 2012 Cape Town Agreement’ to enhance the safety of fishing vessels and related issues in 
the Arctic. The project shares the experience gained in the implementation process of the Agreement by Arctic 
States and other nations, recognizing the importance of fishing vessel safety in the Arctic due to the increased 
traffic of fishing vessels in the region. 
 
POLARIS review 
 
MSC 96 approved MSC.1/Circ.1519 on Guidance on methodologies for assessing operational capabilities 
and limitations in ice. The POLARIS methodology was agreed at IMO as ‘interim guidance’ providing for a 
review four years after the entry into force of the Polar Code in 2017, in order to make any necessary 
amendments based on experience gained. It was therefore agreed that that the future review of the Guidance 
should be undertaken by the SDC Sub-Committee, without a need for a new output, under the existing output 
on “Consequential work related to the new Code for ships operating in polar waters”. To date no review has 
taken place, and this will require a formal proposal. 
 
In order to facilitate this work, IMO with Canada are co-leading PAME’s ‘POLARIS Review’ Project. 
 
Places of refuge 
 
Additionally, IMO and the United States are co-leading PAME's project to compile an inventory of potential 
places of refuge for ships in the Arctic in need of assistance.

Page 6 of 7 

If applicable, please describe in no more than one page your State’s or Organization’s 
future plans for contributing to the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task 
Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Please highlight intentions to contribute to specific projects 
and to collaborate with Permanent Participants. 
 

The IMO Secretariat will continue to participate in meetings of the Arctic Council and its working groups and 
facilitate the exchange of information between the two bodies, including in-kind support and the hosting of 
meetings such as the 2025 Polar Maritime Seminar and future Arctic Shipping Best Practice Information 
Forum meetings. IMO remains committed to completing the ongoing PAME projects in which IMO is a co-lead 
and aims to identify future projects to which IMO can provide support. In all engagements in Arctic Council 
projects IMO endeavours to fully involve Permanent Participants. 
 
By means of IMO's Integrated Technical Cooperation (ITC) Programme, the Organization assists Member 
States in need of capacity-building for the implementation of IMO instruments, including SOLAS, MARPOL, 
STCW and STCW-F Conventions and the Polar Code. An example of such ITC activity is the cooperation 
between IMO and Transport Canada. By means of a Memorandum of Understanding, the two organizations 
have been delivering regional capacity-building workshops around the world in order to train instructors in the 
preparation and delivery of training programmes for seafarers on ships operating in polar waters and the 
effective implementation of the Polar Code. Two workshops were delivered in 2019, two further 
eLearning/virtual workshops were delivered in in 2021, and a hybrid e-learning/in person workshop was 
delivered in 2022. In December 2023, an international workshop to review lessons learned over the course 
of this training programme was held in Argentina, engaging many delegates who had previously participated 
in the regional train-the-trainer workshops. This work has produced recommendations for further work that 
will be taken into consideration during the revision of the STCW Convention. Discussions are on-going in 
relation to the continuation of the capacity-building workshops, given the success of the initial activities. 
 
Arctic Council Member States, Permanent Participants, and Observer Organizations are invited to indicate 
their interest in collaborating with IMO in order to deliver future joint activities, such as the aforementioned 
cooperation with Canada. Such collaboration can cover all aspects of IMO's regulatory work so as to improve 
implementation of IMO's instruments and could include, among others, providing expertise to IMO's ITCP, 
contributing financially in order to develop training material or the hosting of national and/or regional events 
for promoting the IMO Polar Code.
